content.content:
vc-x1 0.85.19-1+ca054252f801.dirty

Create a project, a dual workspace or a plain repo with -s por

Usage: vc-x1 init [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --target <URL|PATH|NAME>
          What to create: URL, path, or bare NAME.
          
          - URL: `git@host:owner/name(.git)?`, `https://...(.git)?`,
            used as-is, config not consulted.
          - Path: `./X`, `../X`, `/X`, `~/X`, `~`, `.`, `..`, is the
            directory path, remote resolved via `--repo` chain.
          - Bare NAME: becomes NAME.git, remote resolved via
            `--repo` chain.
          
          A slashed target with no path prefix (`owner/name`) is
          refused: it reads equally as a path and as the retired
          owner/name shorthand, so pass `./owner/name` or a URL.

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --test-repo <PATH>
          Make a throwaway test repo at PATH, `<path>/<repo-name>`, that
          nothing leaves this machine from.
          
          The workspace is PATH and its bare remotes are beside it in
          `PATH.remotes`, so several test repos share a directory. No
          `~/.claude/projects` symlink is made. In place of `--target`,
          and not with what names a remote or an existing directory.

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --name <NAME>
          Repo directory name override (URL form only).
          
          - URL form: repo created at `cwd/<NAME>` instead of the
            URL-derived name.
          - Path / bare-NAME forms: error if given (TARGET already
            names the repo).

      --account <NAME>
          Account name: picks `[account.<a>]` from user config.
          
          - Without this flag, `[default].account` (or top-level
            `[repo]` shorthand) is used.
          - Meaningful only with Path or bare-NAME targets, since a
            URL target supplies the remote directly.

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --repo <CAT[=VAL]>
          Repo target: `<cat>` or `<cat>=<val>`.
          
          - `<cat>` looks up the value via the account chain
            in the user config.
          - `<cat>=<val>` uses the literal value, no config
            lookup needed.
          - Specific category meanings (`remote`, `local`,
            ...) depend on the consumer subcommand.

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          What to create, `b|both` a dual workspace (work + agent repo) or
          `p|por` a plain single repo [default: both]
          
          [possible values: both, por]

      --dry-run
          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

      --private
          Create private GitHub repos (default: public).
          
          - Only meaningful when the resolved provisioner is
            `gh repo create` (GitHub URL or `--repo remote` whose
            value points at GitHub).

      --push-retries <PUSH_RETRIES>
          Max push retries after repo creation [default: 5]
          
          [default: 5]

      --push-retry-delay <PUSH_RETRY_DELAY>
          Seconds between push retries [default: 3]
          
          [default: 3]

      --use-template <WORK[,BOT]>
          Seed repos from template directories.
          
          Value is `WORK[,BOT]`. Default bot path is `<CODE>.claude`
          (file-name concat, not path join: templates are siblings).
          
          - With `-s por`: only `WORK` is used; passing `,BOT`
            is fatal (no bot side to seed).
          - Non-hidden contents copied recursively; hidden entries
            (names starting with `.`) are skipped: init writes its
            own hidden files.
          - If a copied tree has a `README.md`, its first line is
            rewritten to `# <repo-name>`.

      --config <none|PATH>
          Override the canned workspace config write.
          
          - Absent: write the canned `.vc-config.md`.
          - `--config none`: skip writing entirely.
          - `--config <path>`: copy `<path>` to `.vc-config.md`, or to
            `.vc-config.toml` for a source that is not markdown
            (bytewise; no schema validation).

      --adopt
          Grow an existing TARGET into a dual workspace rather than refuse it.
          
          TARGET may be a plain directory, a repo with no workspace config, or a
          single-repo workspace. A dual workspace is refused, having nothing to
          grow.

      --no-url-trailer
          Stamp the work commit's `ochid:` alone, with no `ocid:` or `pcid:`
          links. A plain repo stamps no trailer, so it changes nothing there

      --agent-dir <DIR>
          The agent repo's directory, one name inside the project directory
          [default: .agent-session]. Dual only

      --agent-repo <NAME>
          The agent repo's full name on its remote. Dual only.
          
          Default: the work repo's name plus `--agent-suffix`.

      --agent-suffix <SUFFIX>
          The suffix the work repo's name takes to name the agent repo on its
          remote, beginning with `.` or `-` [default: .agent-session]. Dual only

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

Your instinct is right: the convert case is the common one, and it's where overwriting hurts. One correction on the command: `init` already has `--adopt`, so converting is `vc-x1 init --target . --adopt`. Without `--adopt`, `init` refuses an existing directory.

**One script, not two.** "New" and "convert" differ only in how `init` runs:
- New project: `vc-x1 init --target foo`, then apply the template to `foo`.
- Existing repo: `vc-x1 init --target . --adopt`, then apply the template to `.`.

So the script does one thing: apply a template to a dual workspace that already exists. It never runs `init`. That keeps it small, and both cases go through the same overwrite checks.

**Name.** Something like `scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh <template> [<workspace>]`. "Apply" says what it does to your files, "copy" only says how, and the `vc-dr-` prefix still reads well if it ends up on your PATH. Keeping it in vc-x1's `scripts/` until it grows is fine, as long as it's clearly a tool shipped beside vc-x1, not part of the binary.

**Overwrite safety, in order of strength:**
1. **Start clean.** Refuse unless both repos' `@` are empty. Then every write shows up as a diff, and `jj restore` undoes all of it. This is the real backstop, and everything below just tries to make sure you never need it.
2. **Never extract into the workspace.** Fetch and unpack into a staging directory under `tmp/`. Reject any template entry that's an absolute path, contains `..`, or is a symlink. Refuse to write through a symlink in the target.
3. **Plan before writing.** Sort every path the template would write into one of three kinds:
   - **new:** the file doesn't exist yet, so it's written.
   - **identical:** the file exists with the same content, so it's skipped silently.
   - **differs:** the file exists with different content, or a file and a directory collide.
   
   Check against what's on disk, not what git tracks, so an untracked or gitignored file (a local `custom.md`, say) counts.
4. **All or nothing.** If anything differs, write nothing, print the plan, and exit nonzero. Never apply half a template.
5. **Ways forward, each explicit:**
   - `--keep-existing` skips the differing files.
   - `--beside` writes `<file>.template` next to each differing file, for a hand merge.
   - `--overwrite <path>` overwrites one named file at a time.
   
   No blanket `--force`.
6. **One automatic merge only: `.gitignore`.** Append the lines it lacks. Line-by-line union is the only merge that can't lose anything. `README.md`, `LICENSE-*`, `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` and `TODO.md` are the likely collisions in a convert, and none of them is merged automatically. An existing `TODO.md` in some other shape especially needs you, since the agent-files require their own format.
7. **No commit.** The script ends by printing each repo's `jj diff --stat` and the `vc-x1 commit` to run after you review. That changes my earlier "the script commits" step, which is too eager for a convert.

`--dry-run` is then just "print the plan from step 3 and stop".

**`init --adopt` owes you the same rule.** I haven't checked what it does to an existing `.gitignore` or `README.md`. The `--use-template` we're removing rewrote a README's first line, which is exactly the kind of quiet edit to avoid. That's worth checking when `--use-template` goes in this rung.

**A side finding for the rung's review.** The `--test-repo` help says "No `~/.claude/projects` symlink is made". The rung's record says it makes one (your catch, 2026-11-02). One of them is stale.

If you agree, I'll update the template Todo with the script's location and name, the apply-only shape, the safety rules above, and no commit.

The plain version: use one script that only applies a template to a workspace `init` has already made, whether that's a brand-new project or an existing repo converted with `--adopt`. It starts only from a clean state, unpacks somewhere separate, and lists every file it would touch. It refuses outright if any existing file would change, unless you say per file what to do. Then it leaves everything uncommitted for you to review.

A test between the steps can leave the next one refused, full `validate`'s `cargo fmt` dirtying the
`@` that `land` needs empty. A test changes nothing the next step depends on, or the step says what it
found and how to go on.

##### feat: close, land, and push say where the cycle stands

Nothing says what state a cycle is in. Each command ends by printing it and what may come next, and
refuses what may not, and `vc-x1 close` arrives.

##### docs: the rules and README name the three steps

The README and **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1**: **A cycle stays local until its Land**, **Land is the
sequence, and `vc-x1 land` its integrate step**, **Only push publishes**, and **Work commits link by
URL** are rewritten, and the Terminology gets a word for what makes a cycle permanent, we think
"release". The rules themselves change in that proposal's cycle.

##### feat: close, land, and push compose with testing closing

Closing out the cycle.

file.content:
#### Solution

Provisional. Three steps, each doing one thing, that compose with testing:

- Every step leaves a state that can be tested, nothing half-done.
- A step may repeat, so the user can test, tweak, and close again.
- Testing does not disturb the cycle or block the next step.
- Each tester's binary says what it is, its suffix the build and its version the commit.
- Exit codes can be trusted, so the steps and the tests chain in a plain shell, and `vc-x1` does not
  run the tests itself.

The steps:

- close makes the cycle's final shape, single-step or a trapezoid, local, with `--scope` defaulting to
  work. It may be run again, and the agent and the user keep iterating on it.
- land merges or fast-forwards onto any bookmark, local, and it may repeat. `--scope` defaults to work,
  and it takes any scope that applies.
- push to any other bookmark shares the work for backup or testing, with `xxxx` still in it. Push to a
  release bookmark with `-s b` seals: it commits the agent `@`, fills the `ocid:`, refreshes any stale
  `pcid:`, checks each tree unchanged, and publishes the agent repo first.
- A release bookmark is one the user treats as permanent: `[release] bookmarks`, or `main` and `master`
  when that key is absent. Work alone with an unsealed agent commit is an error there, unless `--yes`.

The links follow one general rule, for any mix of work and agent commits:

- `ochid:` is one line per related commit, on either side.
- Every `ocid:` is the SHA of an agent commit the same commit's `ochid:` lines name, matched by
  resolving it and not by line order.
- A work commit's `ocid:` is real only when its agent commit was made before it, wink's (2026-11-02),
  and otherwise stays `xxxx`. So most are `xxxx`, rungs included and on a release bookmark, and are
  never rewritten. In an N:1 cycle only the closing has a real one, the seal committing the
  agent repo before
  the closing's final form. In 1:1 pairs every commit has a real one.
- Each agent commit's SHA is carried by exactly one work commit, the last it names.

#### Acceptance check

content.text:
Your invocation can work with a small change. Most of the plumbing is already there, because `--test-repo P` is just shorthand inside `init` (`src/init/params.rs:79`):

```
--test-repo P  ==  --target P  --repo local=P.remotes   (plus local-only guards)
```

So `vc-x1-dev init --target ./wt4 --repo local=./remotes` already puts the remotes in `./remotes`, with one catch. `--repo local` names the bare repos `remote-work.git` and `remote-work.agent-session.git` no matter what the project is called (`src/init.rs:1261`). A second test repo in the same `./remotes` would collide with the first. That's why `--test-repo` gave each repo its own `P.remotes` directory.

**What I'd do:**
- **`--test-repo <REMOTES>` always names the remotes directory, and `--target` is required beside it.** One meaning for the value, and your command works exactly as typed. The old form, where the value was the workspace path with `P.remotes` beside it, goes away.
- **Bare repos are named after the project:** `./remotes/wt4.git` and `./remotes/wt4.agent-session.git`. Many test repos can then share one remotes directory. If either name already exists, init refuses.
- **The local-only guards stay:** a URL target, `--repo`, `--account` and `--private` are still refused, so nothing leaves the machine.
- **`--repo local` keeps its fixed names.** Changing it would touch `clone`'s round trip and the fixtures. It's a separate decision and doesn't belong in this rung.

**One opening worth considering: allowing `--adopt`.** Your likeliest real use is converting an existing repo. `--test-repo ./remotes --target ./copy-of-x --adopt` would let you rehearse that, and later `vc-dr-apply.sh`, on a copy with local remotes. The risk is that an adopted repo may already have an `origin` pointing at GitHub. That breaks "nothing leaves this machine" unless init either refuses such a repo or replaces its `origin`. I haven't checked what `--adopt` does with an existing `origin`.

**Where it goes:** this reshapes the feature the current rung adds, so I'd fold it into **feat: init --test-repo makes a test repo** rather than add another rung.

Three things to confirm before I start:
1. Is `--test-repo <REMOTES>` with `--target` required the shape you want, dropping the alone form?
2. Should bare repos be named `<name>.git` and `<name>.agent-session.git`?
3. Should `--adopt` be allowed now, which means checking how it handles an existing `origin`, or left as a Todo?

The plain version: `init` can already put a test repo's remotes in a separate directory, but it gives the remotes fixed names, so two test repos would collide there. I'd make `--test-repo` mean "the remotes directory", require `--target` for the workspace, and name the remotes after the project so many can share one directory. That fits inside the rung you're testing.

4	//! from. Built `From<&InitArgs>` at the binary edge (main.rs);
5	//! callers without clap (tests, future TUI / library embedding)
6	//! construct it directly.
7	//!
8	//! Per `notes/chores/chores-09.md > ## InitParams implementation
9	//! (0.44.0)`: domain types pass through (`RepoSelector`,
10	//! `ConfigKind`, `PushRetryOptions`); leaf clap wrappers do not.

12	use crate::config::RepoSelector;
13	use crate::init::InitArgs;
14	use crate::options_flags::config::ConfigKind;
15	use crate::options_flags::push_retry::PushRetryOptions;

17	/// Inputs to the init op, flat, owned, clap-free.
18	///
19	/// - `target`: `--target` (URL, path, or
20	///   bare NAME).
21	/// - `name`: optional `--name` override.
22	/// - `account`: `--account` value (None => default account chain).
23	/// - `repo`: `--repo` value parsed into a `RepoSelector`.
24	/// - `por`: `-s` resolved, `true` for `por`, a plain single repo,

26	/// - `private`: `--private`.
27	/// - `dry_run`: `--dry-run`.
28	/// - `push_retry`: `--push-retries` / `--push-retry-delay`.
29	/// - `use_template`: `--use-template` value.
30	/// - `config`: resolved `--config` value (None => canned write).
31	/// - `adopt`: `--adopt`, grow an existing target.
32	/// - `agent_dir`, `agent_repo`, `agent_suffix`: the `--agent-*`
33	///   flags, None meaning the default (dual only).
34	/// - `create_symlink`: whether `init` should create the
35	///   `~/.claude/projects/` symlink for dual runs (production
36	///   path = true; test fixtures suppress with false).
37	pub struct InitParams {
38	    pub target: String,

# Commit model

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as
specimens rather than a skeleton: a work rung's body and a bookend's. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form).

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

The intro states this commit's problem and defines "split", the word the title assumes. Each `*`
is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
diff already lists.

## A bookend

Title: `refactor: extract config loader opening`

```
Opens the cycle "refactor: extract config loader". Its record is the
In Progress block in TODO.md.
```

A bookend resolves no problem of its own, so its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the
cycle by its title and pointing at its record. The closing's body is the same shape with "Closes".

content.content:
90	### Line widths
91	
92	Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather than
93	restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated 2026-08-09,
94	when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.
95	
96	- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
97	- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
98	  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
99	- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
100	- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
101	  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.
102	
103	The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps when
104	touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than imitating the
105	narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL, a literal report
106	row, indented code in a comment).
107	
108	### Problem-first shape
109	
110	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same
111	shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.
112	
113	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
114	  follows it.
115	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering
116	  whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in [Bullet content
117	  differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
118	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
119	  - In Progress: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See [Conventional-commit
120	    shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) for the per-step title + `(current)` /
121	    `(done)` form.
122	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is picked up
123	    into a cycle.
124	
125	**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A cycle
126	writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's commit
127	body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a commit body's
128	is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule here said a plan
129	was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle unable to say at its
130	opening what it intended to do.
131	
132	### Commit-body form
133	
134	The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
135	shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
136	problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
137	bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
138	statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.
139	
140	- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
141	  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
142	  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the

### Line widths

Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather than
restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated 2026-08-09,
when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.

- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.

The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps when
touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than imitating the
narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL, a literal report
row, indented code in a comment).

### Problem-first shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same
shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.

- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
  follows it.
- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering
  whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in [Bullet content
  differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
  - In Progress: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See [Conventional-commit
    shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) for the per-step title + `(current)` /
    `(done)` form.
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is picked up
    into a cycle.

**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A cycle
writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's commit
body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a commit body's
is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule here said a plan
was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle unable to say at its
opening what it intended to do.

### Commit-body form

The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.

- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
  to be more than one commit.
- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
  form, the general form at its smallest.
- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.

**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are
read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.

Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit).

# Convert an existing plain directory into a dual workspace
vc-x1 init --target . --adopt

# Name the agent repo's directory and its remote
vc-x1 init --target my-project --agent-dir .sessions --agent-suffix -sessions
vc-x1 init --target my-project --agent-repo my-project.claude

# Seed both repos from template directories (sibling layout)
vc-x1 init --target my-project --use-template \
    ../vc-x1-work-repo-template,../vc-x1-bot-repo-template

# BOT omitted defaults to the `<CODE>.claude` sibling
vc-x1 init --target my-project --use-template ../tmpl
# Equivalent to:
vc-x1 init --target my-project --use-template ../tmpl,../tmpl.claude
```

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--target <URL\|PATH\|NAME>` | What to create: a URL, a path, or a bare NAME, required |
| `--test-repo <REMOTES>` | Make the target a throwaway test repo, its remotes `<name>.git` and `<name>.agent-session.git` in REMOTES, so test repos share it |
| `--name <NAME>` | Repo directory name override (URL form only) |
| `--account <NAME>` | Pick `[account.<a>]` from user config |
| `--repo <CAT[=VAL]>` | Repo target, e.g. `local=<PARENT>` for local bare remotes |
| `-s, --scope <SCOPE>` | `both`, a dual workspace, or `por`, a plain single repo (no agent repo) [default: both] |
| `--adopt` | Convert an existing TARGET into a dual workspace (see below) |
| `--no-url-trailer` | Stamp the work commit's `ochid:` alone, with no `ocid:` or `pcid:` links |
| `--agent-dir <DIR>` | The agent repo's directory, one name [default: .agent-session] |
| `--agent-repo <NAME>` | The agent repo's whole remote name |
| `--agent-suffix <SUFFIX>` | The work repo's name plus this names the agent repo [default: .agent-session] |
| `--private` | Create private GitHub repos [default: public] |
| `--dry-run` | Show what would be done without executing |
| `--push-retries <N>` | Max push retries after repo creation [default: 5] |
| `--push-retry-delay <N>` | Seconds between push retries [default: 3] |
| `--use-template <ROOT\|CODE[,BOT]>` | Seed both repos from template dirs (see below) |
| `--config <none\|PATH>` | Override the canned config write, under the name the source's carrier calls for |

**`--use-template`**. Value is `ROOT` or `CODE[,BOT]`. A `ROOT` is a directory holding `work/` and
`agent/`, which it names both of. Otherwise, if `BOT` is omitted, it defaults to the sibling directory
`<CODE>.claude` (file-name concat, not path join, since the two templates are not nested). Each path
expands `~` and `$VAR`.
Non-hidden contents are copied recursively into each target, and hidden entries (names starting with
`.`) are skipped since init creates the repo's own hidden files (`.vc-config.md`, `.gitignore`,
`.git/`, `.jj/`). If either template has a `README.md` at its root, its first line is rewritten to
`# <repo-name>`: `<name>` for the work repo and `<name>.claude` for the bot repo. For local
verification without hitting GitHub, combine `--use-template` with `--repo local=<PARENT>`.

**`--adopt`**. Without it an existing TARGET is refused, named by what it holds. With it, init
grows the target into a dual workspace:

- A plain directory, no repo: both repos are created around it, and everything in it that its
  `.gitignore` does not exclude is the work repo's first commit, whatever the file sizes. Files
  over jj's new-file size limit (1MiB by default) are listed, since jj would otherwise leave them
  out. A `.gitignore` it already has is kept and given the lines it lacks, the agent directory's
  and `/.claude/settings.local.json`.
- A jj repo colocated with git and with no workspace config: its history stays, and one commit,
  "Adopt as a dual-repo workspace", goes on top, carrying `.vc-config.md`, the `.gitignore` lines,
  and the `ochid:` trailer to the agent repo's first commit. With an `origin`, the agent repo's
  remote is derived beside it, `--repo` and `--account` are refused, and the work side pushes
  nothing: the commit is yours to land. With no origin, the remotes come from `--repo` as for a
  fresh init, and both are pushed. A working copy with uncommitted work is refused, and a git-only
  repo is pointed at `jj git init --colocate`.
- A single-repo workspace, one whose config declares `repos.work` alone, such as `init -s por`
  makes: adopted as the repo above, except that its config is edited in place. `agent =` goes into
  `[repos]` and `agent-repo =` under `[remote]`, and every other line, prose and comments
  included, stays as it was.
- A dual-repo workspace is refused, having nothing to grow.

`--adopt` is refused with `-s por` and with `--use-template`, and on a `--target` that does not
exist. The old `<TARGET> [NAME]` positionals are refused, naming `--target` and `--name`, and
`--por` is refused, naming `--scope por`.

Requires `gh` (authenticated) and `jj` to be installed (`gh` is skipped under `--repo local=...`).

  `--adopt` the chain's error is held and raised only when the target has no origin.
- A single-repo workspace's config is edited by adding lines only, `agent =` after the last key of
  `[repos]` and `agent-repo =` under `[remote]`, with prose, comments, and other keys untouched.
  The file is read back and restored when it does not declare both keys.
- An adopted directory's `.gitignore` is kept and given the lines it lacks, the agent directory's
  and `/.claude/settings.local.json`, Claude Code's local project settings file.
- The first commit tracks every file whatever its size, since jj leaves a new file over
  `snapshot.max-new-file-size` untracked, and names the ones over the limit.
- `--use-template` is refused with `--adopt`, since a template would overwrite files of the same
  name.

cross-repo migration" (rest folded into the 0.72.0 merge close-out cycle's docs step): in a
multi-contributor flow, ochids change at every merge until the change reaches the canonical repo's
`main`, so document the migration story.

Attach an agent companion plus `.vc-config.md` to an existing por workspace as a routine
subcommand, described in [the stage](refactor-20260716.md#stage-por--dual-conversion). Last program
stage on purpose, since it leans on facade-owns-topology and the in-process init pieces.

### `init` template ergonomics

Take-or-leave ideas from the template restructure (mailbox, 2026-07-31), triaged here 2026-08-02:
- `--use-template <repo-root>` auto-detecting `work/` / `work.claude/`, so the caller passes the
  template repo rather than its payload subdirectory
- a no-remote init mode for local testing
- an empty-dir agent template only needs a `.gitkeep`, since init writes hidden files itself

### Warn on the legacy `[workspace]` schema from any command

A repo on the old schema reads, logs, and diffs fine for weeks and discovers the problem only when
`push` hard-errors, the least convenient moment. Cheap fix: any command warns once on a legacy
config rather than only `config --validate` and `push`. iiac-perf finding (mailbox, 2026-08-07).

### Revset pass-through: stop translating the house dialect

- With it, the schema could mark the command lists `kind = "command-list"` beside `path`, so
  `config --validate` checks a list's placeholders without running it.

### Improve init and add rename and delete subcommands

(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) A workspace's name is written into six places, and nothing renames or
removes them together: the work-repo's directory, the agent-repo's directory when it is not
nested, the two repos on the remote, each repo's `origin` URL, the `.vc-config.{toml|md}` of both
sides, and the Claude Code symlink. And `init` makes a workspace it cannot always finish, or that
Claude Code does not find.

- The order is wink's: `init` is fixed first, then `vc-x1 delete`, then `vc-x1 rename`. Each is a
  cycle of its own.
- The `init` work is more than one cycle, wink's order: the agent template `--use-template` looks
  for first, then the path over 200 characters, then the name GitHub would change, the order the
  three parts below are in.
- Delete is ahead of rename: its "find every part of a workspace from its config" is what rename
  reuses, and it gives `init` the cleanup it lacks.
- The parts are `####` headings, where [Todo format](agent-data/notes.md#todo-format) asks for
  bullets with a bold title, since a heading is an anchor a link can name.
- Delete leans on two entries far down this list: the clean verdict of [status prints a verdict
  per repo and exits with a bit per
  side](#status-prints-a-verdict-per-repo-and-exits-with-a-bit-per-side), and [status reports the
  commits no bookmark reaches](#status-reports-the-commits-no-bookmark-reaches). Whether they move
  up ahead of it, or delete's cycle builds the verdict as its first rung, is open.
- One experiment wants wink starting a fresh Claude Code session, the symlink's below.

#### init --use-template takes an existing workspace as the template

(wink, 2026-10-09) Someday an existing work directory should serve as a template. Today
`--use-template WORK` requires an agent template too, defaulting to the sibling directory
`<WORK>.claude`, and a workspace has no such sibling: its agent-repo is nested inside it and holds
session data, which is nothing to copy.

```
$ vc-x1 init io-uring-2-zcr-v4-x2 --use-template io_uring-2-zcr-v4-x1/
vc-x1 0.84.15
Preflight checks...
error: --use-template: agent template 'io_uring-2-zcr-v4-x1.claude' does not exist
```

Met again 2026-10-11 at 0.84.21, the same command and the same error, the template a workspace
whose agent-repo is the nested `.agent-session`.

- The agent template becomes optional: the sibling when it exists, otherwise an agent-repo seeded
  with nothing.
- The sibling default still ends in `.claude`, and whether it follows the `.agent-session` rename
  is decided with the template repo, where the short-term fix, updating its `work` and
  `work.claude`, is being made.

2930	  (2026-07-29), where fixing that commit's own close-out bookkeeping meant editing content *and*
2931	  message, and the trailer survived only by hand-copying it. `vc-x1 fix-desc` can repair a dropped
2932	  ochid by title match, so the failure is recoverable, not silent-forever.
2933	- Amending a just-pushed commit is a real workflow, not a rare one: the cycle-record cites no SHA by
2934	  design, so a rewrite costs nothing. Message fixes naturally cluster there, which is exactly where
2935	  the two-step shape bites.
2936	
2937	### Restructure templates: one repo + a fixed agent seed manifest
2938	
2939	Replace the separate `vc-x1-work-repo-template` + `vc-x1-bot-repo-template` repos with the one
2940	work-repo template, whose live `.claude/` doubles as the agent-side seed source, and retire
2941	`vc-x1-bot-repo-template`. `vc-x1 init` / `clone` updates for the new layout. First up after the
2942	refactor program.
2943	- `--use-template` rule: explicit `CODE,BOT` copies all non-hidden files from BOT (unchanged, the
2944	  escape hatch for rich agent seeds), and `CODE` alone seeds the agent side from a fixed manifest
2945	  (`LICENSE-*`, `README.md`) taken from `<CODE>/.claude/`. The `<CODE>.claude` sibling default is
2946	  dropped.
2947	- The manifest is the safety property: a live `.claude` has non-hidden session artifacts at top
2948	  level, and the known subset is what lets it double as the seed source without leaking session
2949	  history into new projects.
2950	- Manifest members missing in the source are skipped, so a code template with no `.claude/` content
2951	  yields a bare-but-valid agent-repo (the agent template is optional, since init already generates
2952	  the true minimum itself).
2953	- `memory/MEMORY.md` moves from copied to generated: it is intentionally empty (seeded only because
2954	  Claude tends to create it otherwise), so init emits it like `.vc-config.md` instead of copying,
2955	  leaving no "is it still empty?" invariant in the template.
2956	
2957	### sync follow-up: extract `move-bookmark` command
2958	
2959	The "put the bookmark / `@` where it belongs" step at the end of sync (reposition logic) is useful

  ochid by title match, so the failure is recoverable, not silent-forever.
- Amending a just-pushed commit is a real workflow, not a rare one: the cycle-record cites no SHA by
  design, so a rewrite costs nothing. Message fixes naturally cluster there, which is exactly where
  the two-step shape bites.

### Restructure templates: one repo + a fixed agent seed manifest

Replace the separate `vc-x1-work-repo-template` + `vc-x1-bot-repo-template` repos with the one
work-repo template, whose live `.claude/` doubles as the agent-side seed source, and retire
`vc-x1-bot-repo-template`. `vc-x1 init` / `clone` updates for the new layout. First up after the
refactor program.
- `--use-template` rule: explicit `CODE,BOT` copies all non-hidden files from BOT (unchanged, the
  escape hatch for rich agent seeds), and `CODE` alone seeds the agent side from a fixed manifest
  (`LICENSE-*`, `README.md`) taken from `<CODE>/.claude/`. The `<CODE>.claude` sibling default is
  dropped.
- The manifest is the safety property: a live `.claude` has non-hidden session artifacts at top
  level, and the known subset is what lets it double as the seed source without leaking session
  history into new projects.
- Manifest members missing in the source are skipped, so a code template with no `.claude/` content
  yields a bare-but-valid agent-repo (the agent template is optional, since init already generates
  the true minimum itself).
- `memory/MEMORY.md` moves from copied to generated: it is intentionally empty (seeded only because
  Claude tends to create it otherwise), so init emits it like `.vc-config.md` instead of copying,
  leaving no "is it still empty?" invariant in the template.

### sync follow-up: extract `move-bookmark` command

The "put the bookmark / `@` where it belongs" step at the end of sync (reposition logic) is useful

1205	(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) A workspace's name is written into six places, and nothing renames or

1209	Claude Code does not find.
1210	
1211	- The order is wink's: `init` is fixed first, then `vc-x1 delete`, then `vc-x1 rename`. Each is a
1212	  cycle of its own.

1215	  three parts below are in.

The `--use-template` rung is done, validated, and installed as `vc-x1-dev`. The diff removes 714 lines and adds 75.

**Code**
- **What's gone:** the `--use-template` option module, its parsing, its checks, the template copy, and the step that rewrote a copied README's first line. `prepare_local_repo` now just creates a directory and runs `jj git init`.
- **Also gone:** the step titles' "then copy template" wording, and `AgentPlan.name`, which only that README rewrite read. The fixtures helper no longer takes a template.
- **A typed `--use-template` is still refused by name**, the same way the retired `--por` is: "--use-template is retired: init makes a bare workspace, and a template is applied to it afterwards". A hidden argument and a test cover this.
- **Tests:** 16 template tests are removed, and the shell-completion case now uses `--test-repo` instead.

**Docs**
- **README:** the template examples, the table row and the `--use-template` paragraph are replaced by a short note that init makes a bare workspace and the flag is refused. The `--adopt` paragraph no longer mentions it.
- **`notes/vc-x1-init.md`:** the `--adopt` and `--use-template` line now says the flag is retired.
- **Todos retired:** **init --use-template takes an existing workspace as the template**, **Restructure templates: one repo + a fixed agent seed manifest**, and the backlog entry **`init` template ergonomics**, whose no-remote mode became `--test-repo`. **Improve init** now lists two parts instead of three.
- **zDOING.md:**
  - continuation notes reset to `_None._`
  - this rung marked `(current)`
  - version bumped to `0.85.19-2`

**The `--adopt` overwrite check:** it already follows the template Todo's overwrite rule:
- an existing `.gitignore` is kept and only given the lines it lacks
- a single-repo config is only added to
- nothing else in the directory is written

The one quiet edit, rewriting a README's first line, belonged to `--use-template` and is gone with it. That's recorded in the rung's subsection.

**Left alone:** the design notes under `notes/design-cli/` and `notes/refactor-20260716.md` still mention `--use-template`, because they record past design.

**One slip along the way:** my first attempt at resetting the notes duplicated part of zDOING.md, because the script matched the wrong "## In Progress". I restored the file from the rung commit with `jj restore` and redid the edit. The diff above is the corrected one.

content.text:
It's the new binary's own completion, and it's clap doing this on purpose, not a stale script. clap_complete's rule (`clap_complete/src/engine/complete.rs:217`) is: hidden flags are dropped from the candidates unless nothing visible matches what you've typed. Then it offers the hidden ones.
- `vc-x1-dev init --<TAB>` lists every flag, and `--use-template` and `--por` aren't among them.
- `--use<TAB>` matches no visible flag, so the hidden `--use-template` is offered, with its doc line "The retired `--use-template`, kept so it is refused by name".
- `--po<TAB>` does the same for the retired `--por`, so this has been true of every retired flag here all along.

Running it then gives the tailored refusal, so the worst outcome is one wasted Enter. Three ways to go:
1. **Leave it (my pick).** It's clap's intended behavior, consistent across all the retired flags, and the fish/zsh description already says it's retired.
2. **Drop the hidden argument.** It wouldn't complete, but typing it gives clap's generic "unexpected argument '--use-template'" instead of the message pointing at what replaced it. That breaks with how `--por` and the positionals are retired.
3. **Hide retired flags from completion entirely.** clap has no switch for this, and completion and parsing share one `Command`, built from the derive. We'd need to edit the `Command` the completion factory builds and strip the retired args. That's doable, but it's a change across the whole CLI, so it would be a Todo, not part of this rung.

Which do you want? If it's 1 or 3, this rung's review is otherwise still open.

content.text:
Yes, quite a few. They fall into four groups.

**1. Retired flags.** These are hidden and refused with a pointer to the replacement, so `--<prefix><TAB>` completes them just as it did `--use-template`:

| Command | Retired flag | Its message points at |
|---|---|---|
| `init` | `--por` | `--scope por` |
| `build`, `install`, `run` | `--dev` | `--profile dev` |
| `config` | `--validate` | `vc-x1 validate-config` (retired at 0.80.6) |

**2. Retired subcommands.** These are hidden, so `vc-x1 <prefix><TAB>` completes them when nothing visible matches, for example `vc-x1 bot<TAB>` or `vc-x1 build-<TAB>`:
- `bot-session`, now `agent-session`
- `validate-bot`, now `validate-agent`
- `build-dev`, `install-dev`, `run-dev`, now `build`/`install`/`run --profile dev`

**3. Retired positionals.** About 20 commands take a hidden `RETIRED` positional so the old positional form is refused with a message naming its flag:
- `init` and `clone` (`<TARGET> [NAME]`)
- `push`, `squash-push`, `commit`, `symlink`, `lookup`, `config`
- `validate-anchors`, `validate-desc`, `fix-desc`, `validate-todo`, `fix-todo`, `agent-session`
- `agent-files copy`, `diff` and `size`
- the rev/count positionals that `list`, `desc`, `chid` and `show` share through `common_args`

These don't show up when you complete a `--` flag. Dropping them only changes the error from "the positional is retired, pass `--file X`" to clap's "unexpected argument 'X'". That message is the same one that caught me earlier today with `validate-anchors`.

**4. Hidden but not retired. These stay.**
- `agent-session`'s eight `--no-<item>` flags (`--no-summary` and others) are the live negations of the `--<item>` flags. They're kept out of the help to keep it short.
- The `--scope` values a command doesn't take are hidden per command. `bot` is a hidden value that's refused as the old name for `agent`, so that one is really retired, and belongs with groups 1 and 2.

By your rule from just now, groups 1 and 2 go, plus the `bot` scope value. Group 3 is your call. Its fix-it messages are the useful ones, but each is another hidden argument to carry. That's a sweep across about 25 commands, unrelated to `init`, so I'd file it as a Todo, **Drop the retired flags, subcommands, and positionals**, rather than add a rung to this cycle. Unless you want it in this cycle?

This rung, with `--use-template` removed outright, is validated (850 tests), installed as `vc-x1-dev`, and still waiting on your review.

content.text:
I like it. vc-x1 already carries the rule set, so making it the source removes the separate template repo altogether. What I found changes the script's shape:

**With vc-x1 as the source, little is copied as-is. Most of it is generated.**

| A new repo needs | Can it come from vc-x1? |
|---|---|
| `AGENTS.md` and `agent-data/` | Yes, the rule set. `vc-x1 agent-files copy` already does this, deletions included |
| `LICENSE-*` (both repos), the agent repo's `memory/MEMORY.md` | Yes, they're generic |
| `TODO.md` | No. vc-x1's holds its own records, so it has to be a skeleton (notes.md already says the set ships one) |
| `custom.md` | No. vc-x1's is gitignored and local, so it's a skeleton too |
| The agent repo's `README.md` | No. vc-x1's says "# vc-x1.claude" and "bot repo", so it gets generated with the new name |
| `.gitignore` lines | Only the generic ones (`/tmp`, `/tmp-durable`, `/custom.md`). vc-x1's `/target` and `/.fixtures` are its own |

So the script becomes: `init` has already run, then copy the rule set from a commit of vc-x1, copy the generic files, write the skeletons, and print what to review. The skeleton texts should live as files beside the script, say under `scripts/vc-dr-apply/`, so they're reviewed like the rules.

**Copy from a commit, not the working tree.** `agent-files copy` reads the source's working tree. During the v0.3.1 cycle, that's exactly when vc-x1's working copy holds half-changed rules. The script should take the set from a named commit, defaulting to `main`, e.g. `git archive main AGENTS.md agent-data`. Then the io_uring repo gets a set that has actually landed, and its first commit can record "vc-x1 at `<sha>`".

**Why it fits the v0.3.1 cycle:**
- **It's about handing the rules to a new adopter.** The Terminology still says "the template repository is still to come", and with this, v0.3.1 can say the source is any adopter's committed set and this script applies it.
- **It makes a natural acceptance check.** After the cycle lands, create the io_uring repo from vc-x1's new `main`. The first repo made from v0.3.1 is the test of v0.3.1.

**What it retires:**
- **The old template repos:** `vc-x1-template`, `vc-x1-template-2` (once checked), and the older `vc-x1-work-repo-template`, `vc-x1-bot-repo-template` and `vc-x1-codex-template`. I saw all three next to vc-x1 in your project directory.
- **`[family] template`:** today it's the default source for `agent-files copy` and `diff`, so v0.3.1 needs a new default, probably the source given as a flag, or a sibling adopter.

Applying a whole template repo (the full-template mode, everything committed) can wait until you actually want a template beyond the rules.

If you agree, I'll rewrite the **vc-dr-apply.sh** Todo to match:
- vc-x1 at a commit is the source
- the generated skeletons live beside the script
- the overwrite guards stay
- the full-template mode is deferred

and add one line to **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1** saying its cycle writes the script and its acceptance check creates the io_uring repo. Both edits go into this rung's commit.

cat > tmp/template-todo.md <<'EOF'
### vc-dr-apply.sh applies vc-x1's rules to a dual workspace

(wink + agent, 2026-11-03) `vc-x1 init` makes a bare dual workspace and stops: the two repos and
their remotes, on GitHub or local and bare with `--test-repo`, `.vc-config.md` with `[repos]` and
`[remote]`, the `~/.claude/projects` symlink, and the first commit. What goes in it is not vc-x1's
problem. A script fills it, `scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh [--from <vc-x1>] [--rev <rev>] [<workspace>]`,
written in the cycle of **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1**, wink's call, and vc-x1 is its source, the
adopter whose committed rules a new repo starts from. The first use is the repo exploring the
io_uring interface.

- One script for both uses, since they differ only in the `init` before it, which the script never
  runs. A new project is `vc-x1 init --target foo`, then the script on `foo`. Converting an existing
  repo is `vc-x1 init --target . --adopt`, then the script on `.`.
- It lives in vc-x1, a tool shipped beside it and not part of the binary, and moves to a repo of its
  own if it grows or becomes an app. "Apply" names what it does to the workspace's files, and the
  `vc-dr-` prefix still reads once it is on the PATH.
- What a new repo takes, little of it copied:
  - Copied from vc-x1 at the commit: the set, `AGENTS.md` and `agent-data/`, and the generic files,
    `LICENSE-*` on both sides and the agent repo's `memory/MEMORY.md`.
  - Written from skeletons kept beside the script, under `scripts/vc-dr-apply/`, so they are reviewed
    like the rules: `TODO.md` in [Todo format](agent-data/notes.md#todo-format), since vc-x1's holds
    its own records; `custom.md`, since vc-x1's is gitignored and local; and the agent repo's
    `README.md`, named for the new repo, since vc-x1's says `vc-x1.claude` and "bot repo".
  - `.gitignore` lines, the generic ones alone, `/tmp`, `/tmp-durable`, and `/custom.md`, never
    vc-x1's `/target` or `/.fixtures`.
  - `.vc-config.md` is `init`'s, never copied.
- From a commit, never the working tree: `vc-x1 agent-files copy` reads its source's working tree,
  which in a cycle changing the rules holds them half changed. The script reads vc-x1 at `--rev`,
  `main` by default, `git -C <vc-x1> archive <sha> AGENTS.md agent-data` and `git show <sha>:<file>`,
  with the ref resolved to a SHA first, and the commit that takes the applied files records "vc-x1 at
  `<sha>`" in each repo, provenance of the project's start, so a later look at what the rules changed
  since is a diff from that SHA. `--from` defaults to the vc-x1 the script sits in.
- Overwriting, the hazard of a convert, guarded in order of strength:
  - A clean start: the script refuses unless both repos' `@` are empty, so every write is a diff and
    `jj restore` undoes them all. The backstop the rest keep from being needed.
  - A staging directory under `tmp/`, never an extraction into the workspace. A staged entry that is
    absolute, holds `..`, or is a symlink is refused, and so is a write through a symlink in the
    workspace.
  - A plan before any write: each path the script would write is new, identical, or differs, a file
    meeting a directory included, judged by what is on disk, so an untracked or ignored file counts.
    New is written, identical skipped.
  - All or nothing: any path that differs writes nothing, prints the plan, and exits nonzero. Nothing
    is ever half applied. `--dry-run` prints the plan and stops.
  - Each way past a difference is explicit: `--keep-existing` skips them, `--beside` writes
    `<file>.vc-dr` beside each for a hand merge, and `--overwrite <path>` takes one named file at a
    time. No blanket `--force`.
  - One automatic merge, `.gitignore`, which takes the lines it lacks, a union of lines being the one
    merge that loses nothing. `README.md`, `LICENSE-*`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and `TODO.md`, the
    likely collisions in a convert, are never merged, `TODO.md` least of all, since the agent-files
    require their own shape of it.
  - No commit: the script ends by printing each repo's `jj diff --stat` and the `vc-x1 commit` to run
    after review.
- `init --adopt` already holds to the same rule, checked in **feat: init drops --use-template**: an
  existing `.gitignore` is given only the lines it lacks, and nothing else is written.
- A shell script, not an xtask: it is language-neutral, as the repos it fills need not be Rust.
- Deferred: applying a whole template repo, every committed file of its work side and a fixed
  manifest of its agent side, from a local path or by GitHub's tarball and contents endpoints, until
  wink wants a template beyond the rules. The design is in this entry's history at **feat: init
  --test-repo makes a test repo**.
- Not a separate app yet: one earns its place by updating a project that drifted from its source, as

Both line numbers are correct. The missing `>` is a known gap that an existing Todo covers.

**Line 105 versus 90.** Each number belongs to a different commit, and the output doesn't say which:
- `work src/init.rs:105` is where the line sits in the revision you asked about. `jj file show -r 4a827490b1313 src/init.rs` has "/// Grow an existing TARGET…" at line 105.
- `commit vorzlzzxrpys src/init.rs:90` is where blame found it in the commit that first wrote it. `jj file show -r vorzlzzxrpys src/init.rs` has the same text at line 90.
- In the agent-side output, the windows (`src/init.rs:90-98`) come from `vorzlzzx`'s diff, so they're in that commit's numbering too.

The 15 lines between came from later commits adding code above it. It's the same line, just two snapshots. The fix is in the output: label each number with its commit, for example `work src/init.rs:105 at 4a827490`, and say "first written at line 90" on the commit row.

**The `>` pointer.** The two directions start from different things:
- Work to agent starts from one work line. Lookup finds the single transcript entry that wrote it and marks that entry with `>` among its neighbours.
- Agent to work starts from one transcript entry, here a `python3` heredoc that edited two files. It has no starting work line to point back to. Today it narrows only to the files the call wrote (`src/init/params.rs`, `src/init.rs`) and prints every hunk of the partner commit in those files. Some of those hunks were written by other calls in the same rung. That's why you see `check_target_state` and the other hunks with nothing marking which lines are this call's.

The existing Todo **lookup narrows a write's work window to its lines and flags a renamed partner** (`TODO.md:2214`) already proposes the fix: keep the added lines whose text the call carries (a heredoc body, a Write's content, an Edit's new string). Your case suggests a better form: keep every hunk, but mark the lines the call carries with `>` instead of `+`. You'd see both the whole change and which part this call made. Here the `/// Grow an existing TARGET…` block would be marked, because the python heredoc contains it verbatim.

Shall I add both points to that Todo? One is the `>` marking in place of dropping hunks. The other is labelling each line number with its commit. It's a `TODO.md` edit, so it would go into the next rung's commit, **feat: a test repo converts an existing repo**.

That's a reasonable expectation. It fails for two reasons, and both can be fixed.

**1. The inverse doesn't know where you started.** Your first lookup read `src/init.rs` at `4a827490`, where the line is 105. The second lookup was given only the transcript line and `-r tqtrxzvx`, an agent-side revision. From there the natural place to show the work side is the partner commit `vorzlzzx`, where the same line is 90. Nothing in the second command says "and show it to me as of `4a827490`", so it can't produce 105.

**2. The two directions don't match up one to one.** Many work lines map to one transcript entry, so the forward direction can mark that one entry with `>`. One entry wrote many lines, here a python heredoc that edited two files. To point at line 105, the inverse would have to know which of those lines you meant, or at least mark all the lines that one call wrote. Today it marks none: it narrows to the files and prints every hunk of `vorzlzzx` in them, including hunks written by other calls in the same rung.

**What would make it round-trip:**
- **A work revision for the inverse.** Something like `--work-rev <rev>`, defaulting to the work repo's `@` as the forward direction defaults to the snapshot. The work lines are then numbered as of that revision.
- **Mark the call's own lines.** Among the partner commit's added lines, mark with `>` the ones whose text the call carries (a heredoc body, a Write's content, an Edit's new string). Then map each one to its line number at the work revision using blame there: a line whose blame is still `vorzlzzx` and whose text matches is the same line. Lines changed or removed since are said to be.
- **The forward output prints the inverse command.** For example: `inverse: vc-x1 lookup --line 222bc372-….jsonl:1150 -r tqtrxzvxurlr --work-rev 4a827490`. Running it marks `> src/init.rs:105-112` among the hunks, and the round trip is exact.

With that, your two commands would show 105 both ways. It replaces the "drop the other hunks" idea in **lookup narrows a write's work window to its lines and flags a renamed partner**, since marking keeps the whole diff visible. And it includes the labelling: each line number carries its revision.

content.text:
vc-x1 is answering a different question from the one you had in mind. Lookup asks "who wrote this line, and what was the agent doing when it did?" It doesn't ask "which agent commit goes with the commit I named in `-r`". Here's each step it took:

1. **Read the line at your snapshot.** `-r 4a827490` (`lpkmkxrk`) only says which version of `src/init.rs` to read. Line 105 there is `/// Grow an existing TARGET into a dual workspace rather than`.
2. **Find the commit that wrote it.** Blame from that snapshot: the line was last changed by `vorzlzzx` (2026-09-21, "feat: init adopt detects the target's state"), where it sat at line 90. `jj file annotate -r 4a827490b1313 src/init.rs` says the same. Nothing after that touched it, so `lpkmkxrk` never comes into it.
3. **Follow the trailer to the agent side.** `vorzlzzx`'s description carries `ochid: /.claude/tqtrxzvxurlr`, in the older path form. That names `tqtrxzvx`, the agent commit pushed with it, which has the same title and was made an hour later. That's the `partner` row.
4. **Narrow to that commit's part of the session.** `tqtrxzvx` added lines 1069 to 1279 of the transcript `222bc372….jsonl`, the stretch of the session since the previous push. That's the `window` row.
5. **Find the call that wrote the line.** Inside that window, lookup searches for the tool call whose text contains the line. It's 1150, a Bash `python3` heredoc that edited `init.rs`. That's the `write` row and the `>`.

So "associated" means the session, and the exact tool call in it, that wrote the line, wherever in history that was. For a line unchanged since September, that's a September session.

If what you wanted was "the agent commit that goes with `lpkmkxrk`", that's a direct lookup of the trailer: `vc-x1 desc -r lpkmkxrk -s b` prints its `ochid:` and the agent commit on the other side, with no line involved. To land on `lpkmkxrk`'s session through lookup, pick a line `lpkmkxrk` itself changed. `jj diff -r lpkmkxrk` shows them.

This answers the line-number question too: 105 is the line's position in your snapshot, and 90 is where the September commit wrote it. If the output had said "at `lpkmkxrk`" on the first row, and "last changed by" on the commit row, this would have been clearer. That's the labelling suggestion from before.

The plain version: lookup traced the line back to the September commit that wrote it, then followed that commit's link to the agent commit pushed alongside it, then found the exact tool call in that session. The `-r` you gave only chose which version of the file to read the line from.

Push first, then start the rung. That way the durable part doesn't depend on how far the rung gets before you go.

**Before the push: fold the lookup Todo edit into the last rung.** `@` currently holds only that Todo rewrite. `feat: init drops --use-template` is still local and unpushed, so folding it in with `vc-x1-dev squash -s w` is allowed (a local cycle's record may be reworked), and it leaves `@` empty. If we push first, that edit stays local, and putting it into a pushed commit later would be a remote rewrite needing approval.

**The push: `vc-x1-dev push -s b`.** That should:
- publish the cycle's bookmark to origin for the first time, with the opening and both rungs on it
- commit the agent `@` (today's session, `qqvvzozm`, the partner the rungs' `ochid:` lines already name) and push the agent repo's `main`

What it changes:
- **`ocid: …/xxxx` stays on the pushed work commits.** A Land won't rewrite published commits, it warns instead. That's the outcome the rung **feat: ocid is real only when the agent commit came first** plans for, so it works with this cycle rather than against it.
- **The pushed rungs become published.** From then on any rework of them is a remote rewrite and needs your approval, like any push.
- **One known quirk:** after a topic push, `land` warns that only the first commit goes stale. That's already recorded for the "say where the cycle stands" rung.

**Then the next rung, `feat: a test repo converts an existing repo`.** It's probably more than "soon" allows:
1. read what `--adopt` does with an existing `origin`
2. decide between refusing it and pointing it at REMOTES
3. lift the `--adopt` refusal under `--test-repo`
4. add tests, then validate and review

I'd do step 1 now, which only reads code, and write what I find into the rung's subsection. If you have to leave mid-rung, I'd write continuation notes in zDOING.md, and you can then run `vc-x1 squash-push -s a` to push the agent side again. The transcript, which holds everything said, then reaches the remote. The rung's uncommitted work-repo edits would stay on this machine only, not lost but not backed up, until the rung commits next session.

If that's the plan, the first step is the `squash -s w` of the Todo edit into `feat: init drops --use-template`. It needs your go, and the push after it needs its own.

content.text:
You're right, and I was wrong about this. I've just read `src/push.rs`, and `vc-x1 push -s b` already does it in the right order:

1. **The agent half first** (`push.rs:~450-513`): commit the agent `@` as the partner, squash, and push the agent repo's `main`. The agent commit's SHA now exists and is on the remote.
2. **Then the work half** (`work_half`, `push.rs:545`): if the work `@-` still has `ocid: …/xxxx` and isn't published, rewrite its description with the agent commit's real SHA (`push.rs:603-607`). Then set the bookmark and push.

So pushing now gives the tip, `feat: init drops --use-template`, a real `ocid:`. Pushing the agent repo first is exactly what makes that possible. My "stays `xxxx` on the pushed commits" was wrong for the tip.

**What stays `xxxx` is the earlier rungs**, the opening and `init --test-repo`. That isn't a limit of the order. They could be filled before the push too, but each fill is a rewrite, and that changes the SHA of every rung above it. That's the problem this cycle opened with: the last Land rewrote 12 commits, "so what was tested is not by SHA what lands". The cycle's design (**ocid is real only when the agent commit came first**) settles it as one agent commit carried by exactly one work commit, the last that names it. All three rungs name the same agent `@` (`qqvvzozm`), so only the tip carries its SHA, and the others stay as tested. The links still hold both ways, since every rung's `ochid:` names the agent change id.

So no order to fix. One thing to watch in the push's output is the line `push work: set the ocid: of @- to the agent commit's SHA`. It confirms the fill happened.

**The sandbox:** I'd keep it on and bypass it for the push commands only. Everything else today ran fine sandboxed. A push needs network access to GitHub and your git credentials, and the sandbox may block either. The narrow way is that I run just the push with the sandbox turned off for that one command, after your approval as usual. If it fails partway, push already handles that: it snapshots and restores the work side when its local step fails, and the agent side is pushed before the work side is touched. Turning the sandbox off for the whole session also works, but it removes the guard from every later command too. If you'd rather run it yourself, `! vc-x1-dev push -s b` puts the output straight into this conversation.

The plain version: the order is already right. Push sends the agent side first, then writes that commit's real SHA into the newest work commit before sending it. Only the older rungs keep the placeholder, and that's on purpose, so commits you've already tested keep the same SHAs. For the sandbox, I'd turn it off just for the push command rather than for the whole session.

content.text:
It can, and push can split cleanly: `-s b` is literally `-s a` then `-s w`. That makes an order where every rung gets the real SHA and nothing published is ever rewritten:

1. **`vc-x1-dev squash -s w`** folds the lookup Todo edit into the tip, `feat: init drops --use-template`. This is local, and leaves `@` empty.
2. **`vc-x1-dev push -s a`** commits the agent `@` as the partner (`qqvvzozm`, which all three rungs' `ochid:` lines name) and pushes the agent repo's `main`. The agent commit's SHA now exists and is on the remote.
3. **`vc-x1-dev trailers --update --dry-run`**, then **`--update`**, over its default range, the commits above the trunk up to `@-`. That's the opening and both rungs, oldest first. Each `ocid:` gets the agent commit's SHA, and each `pcid:` its parent's new SHA. None of them is published yet, so there's no topic-bookmark warning, and each tree is checked unchanged.
4. **`vc-x1-dev push -s w`** publishes the cycle's bookmark. The tip's `ocid:` is already real, so push's own fill step finds nothing to do.

Steps 2 and 4 are pushes, each needing your go and the per-command sandbox bypass.

**The cost:** the three rungs get new SHAs, with identical trees. So what you tested holds by content but not by commit id. For example, the installed `vc-x1-dev` reports `ad3f6a23`, which would no longer exist. That's minor here.

**The design point:** it goes against what this cycle's Solution currently says, "Each agent commit's SHA is carried by exactly one work commit, the last it names", and against "most are `xxxx` … and are never rewritten". That rule existed to keep tested SHAs stable. Your approach keeps the trees identical instead and makes every link resolvable. I think yours is the better trade before publishing: rewriting unpublished commits whose trees are checked unchanged costs nothing that matters, and the reader gets a real link on every rung. If you agree, the rung **feat: ocid is real only when the agent commit came first** gets reshaped around "fill every unpublished rung's `ocid:` once the agent commit exists, then publish". Push could even do step 3 itself between its two halves. I'd record that in the cycle's Deliberation when we get to that rung.

If that's the order, step 1, the local squash, is first and needs your go.

content.text:
Agreed on all three.

**1. One command.** `trailers --update` belongs inside push, between its two halves, so `vc-x1 push -s b` becomes:
1. the agent half: commit the agent `@` as the partner and push the agent repo's `main`
2. fill every unpublished work commit's `ocid:` and `pcid:`, oldest first, trees checked unchanged
3. the work half: publish the bookmark

That replaces push's current step of filling only `@-`. It's the natural reshaping of the rung **feat: ocid is real only when the agent commit came first**, and the close and land rungs then compose with it.

**2. No `squash-push -s a` after a real `ocid:`.** Once the work commits carry the agent commit's SHA, that agent commit is frozen. Squashing the trailing session into it changes its SHA, and every `ocid:` naming it then dangles. So whatever the transcript gains after the push (the push's own tool result, my "Published", any later recap) stays in the agent `@`. The next push commits it as a new commit, the start of the next partner. Two consequences:
- **push's agent half** has a "fold the journal into a committed one" path, and it must never fold into a commit whose SHA a work commit names. It should make a new commit instead.
- **The At rest rule in `AGENTS.md`**, whose step 2 is "the user squash-pushes", changes. The tail is left for the next push. That's an agent-files change, so it's for **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1**.

**3. The sandbox experiment.** My prediction is that the leftover is never zero. The push commits the transcript up to the push call, and its tool result and my final message are written after it. We think the recap you see after a few idle minutes is Claude Code's own summary entry, added to the transcript whether or not the sandbox is on. What the sandbox might add is extra entries, or files like the `.claude/.cc-writes` that showed up in `wt4`'s work tree, which is outside the agent repo entirely. It's worth measuring after each "Published", once straight away and once after a few idle minutes:
- `jj -R .agent-session diff --stat`: how much the agent `@` gained
- the new transcript lines by kind (tool result, assistant text, system, summary). A quick `jj -R .agent-session diff --git` with a count of added lines gives the size.
- `jj st` in the work repo, for anything like `.claude/.cc-writes`

Run it with the sandbox on and with it off, keeping everything else the same. If it's off and the agent repo really is clean, that would mean the transcript writes are timed differently than I think, which is worth knowing too.

**For the push in hand,** it can still be done by hand as `squash -s w`, `push -s a`, `trailers --update`, `push -s w`, all four rungs then getting real links. The alternative is waiting until push composes it, and that's your pick. Either way, after the final push the tail stays in the agent `@` and nobody squashes it.

  step, the user's `vc-x1 squash-push -s a`, goes. What the transcript gains after the final push,
  the push's tool result, the "Published", a recap, stays in the agent `@`, and the next push commits
  it as a commit of its own.

A squash after the push rewrites the commit the links point at, wink's finding (2026-11-03).

- `vc-x1 push -s b` commits the agent `@` and pushes it, then rewrites every unpublished work commit's
  `ocid:` to that commit's SHA and its `pcid:` to its parent's, oldest first, each tree checked
  unchanged, as `vc-x1 trailers --update` does, and then publishes the bookmark, one command doing all
  of it. It replaces "each agent commit's SHA is carried by exactly one work commit, the last it
  names" in the cycle **feat: close, land, and push compose with testing**.

##### Why: every link resolves

A rung left at `xxxx` links nothing, and rewriting commits no one else has, their trees unchanged,
costs only their SHAs, wink's (2026-11-03).

"""
s = s.replace(anchor, add + anchor)
open(p, "w").write(s)
EOF

content.content:
### The per-rung flow

Every commit (opening, each rung between, closing) goes through these steps, read from here
immediately before acting ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#the-per-rung-flow)):

0. Sync: sync both repos ([Sync](#sync)), required at the opening and the closing, optional
   between, the agent's or the user's call.
1. Mark current: mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Bump: bump the version-of-record to this commit's version ([Suffix
   scheme](agent-data/versioning.md#suffix-scheme)), the agent-files version beside it in an
   `agent-files` proposal cycle.
3. Work: do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop ([Stop and
   ask](#stop-and-ask)).
4. Rung subsection: write what this rung changed, conceptually, into its subsection under the
   ladder. The rung stays `(current)` until step 7.
5. Validate: `vc-x1 validate` before every review, doc-only commits included. The full run rewrites
   files (`cargo fmt`), so use `--fast` while a review iterates. A failure is read and its cause
   named before validation runs again, and a failure that does not repeat is a finding, reported
   and given a Todo entry.
6. Work review: stop before writing any description and say "please review", as its own message with
   no title or body. Iterate until the user says "continue" / "go". The review is of the
   working-copy diff ([jj basics](agent-data/jj.md#jj-basics)).
7. Flip and describe: flip `(current)` to `(done)` the moment "done" is true, then write the
   description in [Commit-body form](agent-data/prose.md#commit-body-form), read from the file first
   with its specimen, [commit-model.md](agent-data/commit-model.md) ([Commit
   description](#commit-description)). A local description can still be changed before the Land, so
   it has no review of its own.
8. Commit: on the go, `vc-x1 commit -s w --title "..." --body "..."`, local ([Committing vs
   pushing](#committing-vs-pushing)). A rung that changes the artifact then installs its dev build,
   so the next rung runs the code just reviewed ([Dev artifact
   name](agent-data/versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)).

### Committing vs pushing

### Commit-body form

The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is two plain paragraphs, and the
rung's subsection in the record holds the full account, so the breakdown is written once.

- **The problem**, and it defines any word the title assumes. It is *this commit's*, never the
  cycle's: a body whose problem outruns what the diff resolves is describing something larger than
  the commit.
- **The solution**, opening "Solution:", ending with the pointer to the record where it is at that
  commit, "See details in TODO.md." No bullets, so a `--body` flag cannot mistake it for an option.
- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
  its body names the cycle by its title, "Opens the cycle ..." or "Closes the cycle ...", with the
  same pointer after it.
